strapline: A former ambassador charged with treason; Kambwili convicted but spared prison; the EU and Lusaka talk; Kamwala's stalls come down; and Banda's third World 11

stories.title: A former ambassador to Switzerland is charged with treason: police say Martha Mwitumwa, 59, plotted with persons unknown between November 2025 and 23 October 2026
stories.excerpt: The Zambia Police Service said on Monday 9 November that it had arrested and charged Martha Lungu Mwitumwa, who represented Zambia in Geneva from 2019, with treason under Section 43(1) of the Penal Code. She is in custody awaiting a court appearance. The charge is an allegation; she has not entered a plea and no response from her or a lawyer has been reported. She becomes the latest person charged with treason since the August election, after the 18 accused in the Mundubile case.

image.label: Section 43(1)
image.caption: Police say a former ambassador prepared, with people they have not identified, to usurp the executive power of the State. She has not yet appeared in court.

body: A retired diplomat who spent two years as Zambia's ambassador in Switzerland has been charged with treason. Police spokesperson Chipo Kaitisha said in a statement issued in Lusaka on Monday 9 November that Martha Lungu Mwitumwa, 59, had been formally arrested and charged with the offence under Section 43(1) of the Penal Code, Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia, Zambia Monitor, News Diggers and The Zambian Observer reported. All three outlets carried the same account of the police statement.

According to that statement, as reported by the three outlets, the alleged offence took place in Lusaka District between November 2025 and 23 October 2026. Police say Ms Mwitumwa acted jointly with other people whose identities are not known and prepared, or endeavoured to carry out, an unlawful plan to usurp the executive power of the State. The statement gave no detail of what the plan is alleged to have involved, named no co-accused and did not say when she was arrested.

body.text: The suspect is currently detained in police custody and is awaiting appearance before the courts of law.
body.attribution: Chipo Kaitisha, Zambia Police Service spokesperson, in a statement issued in Lusaka on Monday 9 November and quoted by The Zambian Observer

body: Ms Mwitumwa was Zambia's Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office at Geneva and ambassador to Switzerland from 2019 to 2021, Zambia Monitor reported. The Observer, which carried a Kalemba report, said she took up the Geneva posting in May 2019 after more than thirty years in government service, with accreditation that also covered international organisations in Vienna, and that her earlier posts included Director for State Functions, Protocol and Public Relations at Cabinet Office, Director for Gender in Development at the Ministry of Gender from 2012 to 2017, and before that a district administrative officer and then district commissioner between 2009 and 2012. She began her career in teaching.

Zambia Monitor added one piece of recent history: in August 2026, during the election period, police detained Ms Mwitumwa and a campaign blogger at a campaign media centre. The government said at the time that the two had been taken in to assist with investigations, and both were later released. None of Monday's reports said whether that episode is connected to the new charge.

Treason charges have been brought repeatedly since the August general election. Human Rights Watch said in a report published on 1 November that 18 people had been charged with treason in the post-election period, two of whom also face sedition charges; the best known are the opposition presidential candidate Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu, two of 18 applicants held at Mukobeko whose constitutional bail application before a three-judge panel of the Lusaka High Court was listed for a final hearing on 5 November after repeated adjournments, with a ruling to follow, Zambia Monitor reported last month. The same report documented 71 cases of what it called arbitrary arrest or prolonged detention; the government has rejected figures of that kind before, and Zambia Monitor reported in September that the Foreign Minister, Mulambo Haimbe, had said official records did not support the detention figures cited by the European Parliament and that the courts, not the executive, decide bail and trial dates.

The government's broader position was restated on Friday 6 November by the Home Affairs Minister, Dr Clement Andeleki, who warned that the state would not tolerate anyone trying to throw the country into disarray and said Zambia was not a banana republic, News Diggers reported. The Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance's acting secretary general, Muhabi Lungu, answered on Monday that the government should not strip citizens of their rights while claiming to enforce the law, and said the alliance had acted within the Constitution. Neither statement referred to Ms Mwitumwa.

Nothing in Monday's reporting records a response from Ms Mwitumwa, her family or a lawyer, and no court date had been published by Monday night. If her case follows the path of the 18 earlier accused, the first contested question will be bail: their application, made to the High Court, was adjourned repeatedly through October and is still awaiting a ruling.

body.title: What the police statement says, and what it does not
items: **Charge** — treason, Section 43(1) of the Penal Code, Chapter 87.
**Period alleged** — November 2025 to 23 October 2026, in Lusaka District.
**Alleged conduct** — preparing or endeavouring, jointly with persons unknown, to usurp the executive power of the State by unlawful means.
**Not stated** — the date of arrest, what the plan is alleged to have been, the identity of any co-accused, or when she will appear in court.

body.confirmed: That the police have charged Martha Lungu Mwitumwa, 59, with treason under Section 43(1), that the alleged period is November 2025 to 23 October 2026, that she is in custody awaiting a court appearance, and that she served as ambassador in Geneva from 2019 — all from the police statement as reported by Zambia Monitor, News Diggers and The Zambian Observer, and from the career details in the Observer.
body.unverified: Everything about the alleged plot itself: what it involved, who else was supposedly party to it and what evidence the police hold. Whether the August detention is connected. Ms Mwitumwa's response. She is presumed innocent; a charge is an allegation that the State must prove in court.

stories.title: Guilty, but not going to prison: Chishimba Kambwili is convicted of unlawful assembly over a 2023 gathering at his gate and given a one-year suspended sentence
stories.excerpt: Lusaka resident magistrate Kawama Mwamfuli found on Monday 9 November that a crowd of 15 to 20 youths who sang at the former minister's Woodlands home on 26 January 2023 had turned a lawful gathering into an unlawful one, and that his role in facilitating it made him liable even though he had told them to stop. The sentence is suspended; The Zambian Observer reported that the magistrate cited his health. No appeal has been reported.

image.label: Woodlands, 26 January 2023
image.caption: The former Roan MP was convicted over a gathering at his own home that the court found had become unlawful because of what the crowd sang.

body: Chishimba Kambwili, the former Information Minister and former Member of Parliament for Roan, was convicted of unlawful assembly in the Lusaka Magistrates' Court on Monday 9 November and sentenced to one year in prison, suspended. Resident Magistrate Kawama Mwamfuli found that the prosecution had proved the charge beyond reasonable doubt, Zambia Monitor reported. The two outlets that covered the judgment differ on one detail: Zambia Monitor said the charge was brought under Section 75 of the Penal Code, The Zambian Observer under Section 74.

The case concerned a gathering at Mr Kambwili's home in Woodlands on 26 January 2023. According to the judgment as reported by Zambia Monitor, between 15 and 20 youths came onto the premises carrying placards and sang a song containing tribal sentiments. Mr Kambwili's media team filmed the scene and the footage was later posted on his Facebook page. The court accepted that he had cautioned the young people against the song and against hate speech, and that he did not join in the singing, but held that by facilitating the gathering he was criminally liable for what it became.

body.text: Lawful at the gate, unlawful inside

body: The magistrate's reasoning, as Zambia Monitor set it out, turned on two points. First, the gathering had started lawfully because the police had been notified in advance, but it became unlawful through the conduct of the participants, which the court found was likely to provoke a breach of the peace. Second, the fact that it took place at a private residence did not put it outside the law on unlawful assembly. Senior Public Prosecutor Lewis Loti of the National Prosecution Authority appeared for the State.

The defence had argued throughout, The Zambian Observer reported, that Mr Kambwili was simply receiving visitors who had come to apologise for earlier political slights, while the State characterised the crowd as an unauthorised assembly aimed at disturbing public peace. The Observer, which described the crowd as disgruntled youths singing about the cost of living, said the magistrate decided against a custodial sentence on account of Mr Kambwili's health; the paper noted that he had often needed help from prison officers to get into court. Under the terms of the judgment as the Observer described them, he will not serve the sentence unless he commits a similar offence within a period the reports do not specify.
Mr Kambwili made no statement to reporters as he left the court, the Observer said, and neither outlet reported whether he intends to appeal.

body.confirmed: The conviction, the suspended one-year sentence, the magistrate's name, the date and place of the gathering, and the court's reasoning on why a notified gathering became unlawful, all from Zambia Monitor and The Zambian Observer.
body.unverified: The exact section of the Penal Code (the two reports differ), the length of the suspension period, and whether an appeal will be lodged.

stories.title: 'There are no perfect democracies': the EU and Zambia hold the dialogue Lusaka asked for in September, and Haimbe asks to comment on the observers' report before it is published
stories.excerpt: At the second EU–Zambia Extraordinary Partnership Dialogue in Lusaka on Monday 9 November, the EU's Africa director, Francesca Di Mauro, said electoral grievances should be settled through fair and impartial courts and offered support for a national process of dialogue and reconciliation. The Foreign Minister, Mulambo Haimbe, asked for the government to be allowed to comment on the Election Observation Mission's findings before its final report is published. Two days earlier the government spokesman had told the mission to leave criminal cases alone.

image.label: Brussels and Lusaka
image.caption: The meeting Zambia requested after the European Parliament's September resolution produced an agreement to work through the observers' recommendations before 2031.

body: Zambia and the European Union sat down in Lusaka on Monday 9 November for a meeting that the government itself had asked for. The second EU–Zambia Extraordinary Partnership Dialogue was requested by Lusaka to discuss what Zambia Monitor described as post-election challenges and a European Parliament resolution on the country's electoral environment. Francesca Di Mauro, Director for Africa at the European External Action Service, led the EU side; the Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe, led Zambia's.

The EU's message, as reported by both Zambia Monitor and News Diggers, was that grievances arising from the August general election should be dealt with transparently, through fair and impartial judicial processes, in full respect of the constitutional rights and duties of citizens and institutions. News Diggers quoted the EU's position that there are no perfect democracies, and that the Union stands ready to support a national process for dialogue and reconciliation "in full respect of Zambia's ownership, institutions and democratic processes". Dr Di Mauro congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election and welcomed the new Cabinet and Parliament, while saying the EU remained concerned about electoral governance, civic space and the political environment, including access to justice and fundamental freedoms, Zambia Monitor reported.

body.text: We welcome this opportunity to engage openly with the Government on electoral governance.
body.attribution: Francesca Di Mauro, Director for Africa at the European External Action Service, at the dialogue in Lusaka on Monday 9 November, quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: Both sides agreed to work towards implementing the recommendations of the EU Election Observation Mission, including those that need legislation or administrative change, ahead of the 2031 general election, with the EU offering technical support, Zambia Monitor reported. Mr Haimbe welcomed the mission's findings as material that could strengthen electoral administration, institutional capacity, transparency and public confidence, and asked that the government be given a chance to formally consider and comment on them before the final report is made public. He also said the partnership should cover regional peace and security, and reaffirmed Zambia's commitment to multilateralism.

body.text: We believe that such engagement would contribute to a balanced appreciation of the electoral environment.
body.attribution: Mulambo Haimbe, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, at the dialogue on Monday 9 November, quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: The road to Monday's meeting runs through September. The European Parliament adopted a resolution on Zambia's post-election situation on 17 September; three days later Mr Haimbe called it premature, because the observers' final report had not yet been published, and said Zambia had not been consulted. In the same statement he asked the EU delegation in Lusaka to convene a formal partnership dialogue with the European Commission and the External Action Service, Zambia Monitor reported at the time. Monday's meeting is the result.

body.text: The mission and the Mundubile trial

body: The meeting came two days after a sharper exchange about the mission's remit. The EU observers said on Thursday 5 November that they would closely follow the trial of Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, and the Chief Observer, Michael McNamara, said the case had what he called an undoubtedly political dimension given that the two men are the most popular opposition leaders, News Diggers reported. Elvis Nkandu, the Chief Government Spokesperson, replied in an interview on Friday 6 November that he did not understand why an election observation mission would take an interest in a trial that had nothing to do with elections, and that the mission should concentrate on election-related matters rather than criminal cases. Neither Monday's reports nor the EU's statement, as reported, mentioned the trial by name.

stories.title: Brooms before breakfast: 150 commandos clear the stretch from the Universal Church to the flyover, and the council says more than 360 illegal stalls at Kamwala are gone
stories.excerpt: The Special Forces Day clean-up announced last week went ahead in Kamwala on Monday 9 November, led by Brigadier General Moses Shapwaya, The Zambian Observer reported. Lusaka City Council said in a statement the same day that it had demolished over 360 makeshift stalls at the Kamwala flyover after notices and reminders to their owners, and that the railway line had been secured, News Diggers reported. The Observer said traders had dismantled many of their own structures before the soldiers arrived.

image.label: Kamwala, 9 November
image.caption: Soldiers, council enforcement teams and traders cleared the area between the Universal Church and the FINDECO flyover on Special Forces Day.

body: The operation that the Special Forces commander promised the Mayor of Lusaka last week was carried out on Monday morning, 9 November. About 150 commandos of the Zambia Army Special Forces, working with enforcement teams from Lusaka City Council, cleared rubbish, blocked drains and makeshift structures from the stretch of Kamwala between the Universal Church and the FINDECO flyover, The Zambian Observer reported. Brigadier General Moses Shapwaya, the Special Forces Commander, led the exercise, which marked the unit's day and its theme for this year of elite service and community work.

The council's account, issued in a statement on Monday and reported by News Diggers on Tuesday 10 November, put a figure on what was removed. Lusaka City Council said it had demolished more than 360 illegal makeshift stalls put up at the Kamwala Flyover Bridge, that the demolition followed earlier notices and several reminders to the owners to take their structures down, and that the railway line through the area had also been secured. The Diggers report said the army's clean-up and the council's demolition were separate parts of the same day's work.

The Observer described a largely cooperative morning. Traders had been warned in advance, it said, and many pulled down their own shacks before the commandos arrived; the soldiers then split into squads with brooms, rakes and wheelbarrows. The paper quoted an unnamed local coordinator thanking traders for their compliance. It reported that the area known as the Blue Tents market was open and clean by the end, but gave no figure for the waste removed or the cost of the operation, and did not describe any confrontation.

The plan had been announced on Thursday 5 November, when Brigadier General Shapwaya called on the Mayor, Chitambala Mwewa, and offered 150 personnel for the Monday, the Observer reported at the time. The Mayor said the help would speed up the council's cleanliness drive and reinforce its campaign against disorder in the city. The Observer's report of Monday's operation noted, without naming anyone, that some political observers had questioned whether elite defence units should be used for municipal tasks.

The question that follows every clearance is whether the traders return. Neither Monday's reports nor the council's statement, as reported, said where the owners of the 360 stalls are expected to trade from now, or whether any of them will be allocated spaces elsewhere.

stories.title: From 20.8% to 100.9% of GDP: Musokotwane makes the case for paying tax at the budget symposium, the Treasury says Vision 2030 is on track, and NGOCC says women are left behind
stories.excerpt: At the 2027 National Budget Symposium at Mulungushi on Monday 9 November, the Finance Minister traced the debt that rose from 20.8% of GDP in 2011 to 100.9% by the end of 2021 and defended the removal of subsidies, while the Secretary to the Treasury, Felix Nkulukusa, said GDP per capita should rise from US$1,318 to US$2,985 even if some mining targets slip. News Diggers reported the minister comparing tax to a funeral contribution, and the NGOCC said the budget's withdrawal of VAT relief on energy-saving appliances will hit female-headed households.

image.label: The debt arithmetic
image.caption: The minister's case for the 2027 budget rests on the debt crisis he says it took five years to escape, and on taxes he says are the price of services.

body: Three days after presenting a K284.8 billion budget on Friday 6 November, Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane went back over why it looks the way it does. Speaking at the 2027 National Budget Symposium at the Mulungushi International Conference Centre on Monday 9 November, the Minister of Finance and National Planning said Zambia's economic priorities were shifting from stabilisation and debt recovery towards investment, productivity and expansion, and that the reforms of the past five years had laid the ground for that, Zambia Monitor reported.

The figures he gave were the ones he has used before, set out in order. Public debt stood at 20.8% of GDP in 2011 and 100.9% by the end of 2021, against a sub-Saharan African average he put at about 24%. By 2022 the country was spending roughly US$2 billion a year servicing debt, up from under US$90 million in earlier years, money that would otherwise have gone to social protection and investment. National poverty rose from 56.4% in 2015 to about 60% in 2022, with rural poverty near 78%. The response, he said, was fiscal stability, external debt restructuring and the removal of poorly targeted subsidies; the fuel subsidy, he argued, had given K1,500 a month to someone spending K3,000 on fuel and K50 to a villager paying K100 for a bus fare.

Felix Nkulukusa, the Secretary to the Treasury, told the same symposium that Zambia remained on course for Vision 2030 even if some targets under the Grow Zambia Agenda take longer than planned. GDP per capita is projected to rise from US$1,318 in 2025 to US$2,985, against population growth he put at 3.4% by 2031; some mining targets could slip by one or two years because investment is being implemented more slowly than expected; and the aim is to bring the poverty headcount from 60% to below 20%, Zambia Monitor reported.

body.text: This means that we are on a good trajectory to achieving our Vision 2030.
body.attribution: Felix Nkulukusa, Secretary to the Treasury, at the 2027 National Budget Symposium in Lusaka on Monday 9 November, quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: News Diggers reported the minister in blunter terms on Monday. Paying tax, he said, means losing money, in the way that contributing to a funeral at home does; the era of donors paying for services was over, and Zambians should be wary of anyone who promised a good life without saying how the economy would grow. He also said the country's maize stocks were enough to feed it until the 2028 harvest. The paper listed the measures the argument is meant to justify: VAT up from 16% to 16.5%, a 39.5% PAYE band on monthly income above K37,000, a five-point rise in corporate income tax on income currently taxed at 20% or less, and higher duty on ceramics.

Not everyone at the receiving end is persuaded. The NGOCC's executive director, Anne Anamela, said the budget leaves marginalised women and girls behind, News Diggers reported on Monday. Her specific complaint is the proposal to end the zero-rating of VAT on energy-saving appliances, which she said would raise living costs for female-headed households and women traders; she also noted that the Anti-GBV Fund remains unfunded and that the Gender Equity and Equality Commission is still not operating. She gave the budget credit for doubling the school feeding programme to K1 billion and for raising the number of households on social cash transfer to 1.6 million.

A third speech on Monday set the production side of the argument. In an address to the Third Zambia Commodities Market Outlook Conference in Lusaka, read for him by the Minister of Trade and Exports, Dr Caroline Kaunda Katotobe, President Hichilema said the next phase after stabilisation should be production, industrialisation, value addition and export-led growth, and set out targets of 10 million tonnes of maize, 3 million tonnes of soya beans, a million tonnes each of wheat and sugar, 10,000 megawatts of generation and 3 million tonnes of copper a year, Zambia Monitor reported. "Zambia is ready to produce more, add greater value and trade more competitively," the speech said.

stories.title: A 180-megawatt plant for a province on a 1972 line: Stanbic and the DBSA are mandated to raise the money for Ngonye Falls, with construction pencilled in for 2027
stories.excerpt: Western Power Company has signed a mandate with Stanbic Bank Zambia and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to structure and arrange the debt for its run-of-river hydropower project on the Zambezi, Zambia Monitor reported on Monday 9 November. The developer calls it the last step before financial close. The outlets disagree on the project's size: the Monitor puts it at US$600 million, International Water Power at US$800 million. Western Province currently depends on a 66kV line built in 1972.

image.label: Ngonye Falls
image.caption: The mandate signed at the Zim-Zam energy conference puts a long-planned Western Province hydropower scheme within reach of financial close.

body: The Ngonye Falls hydropower project, planned for years on the Zambezi in Western Province, has its lenders' arrangers. Western Power Company (WPC) signed a mandate agreement with Stanbic Bank Zambia and the Development Bank of Southern Africa (DBSA) at the Zim-Zam Energy Summit in Livingstone, making the two institutions responsible for structuring and raising the debt for the scheme, Zambia Monitor reported on Monday 9 November, citing a statement issued that day. International Water Power, which reported the signing on 4 November, listed three co-mandated lead arrangers: Standard Bank South Africa, Stanbic Bank Zambia and the DBSA.

The plant is a 180-megawatt run-of-river scheme. According to the Monitor, the financing will cover both the power station and a 110-kilometre, 220-kilovolt transmission line to connect it to the national grid, in a province that currently relies on a 66kV line built in 1972. The two reports differ on the overall cost: Zambia Monitor describes a US$600 million project, International Water Power a US$800 million development. Neither explains the gap, which may reflect whether the transmission line and development costs are counted.

body.text: The Ngonye Falls Hydropower Project is an important investment in Zambia's energy future.
body.attribution: Sherill Byrne, Head of Project Finance at Standard Bank, in the statement reported by Zambia Monitor on Monday 9 November

body.text: Who is behind it and when it would run

body: The project is being developed jointly by African Power Projects, the Private Infrastructure Development Group and Lunzua Power, the Monitor said; WPC's managing director, Tom Younger, also thanked the Barotse Royal Establishment and PIDG's InfraCo arm for their backing, International Water Power reported. Construction is expected to begin in 2027 once financial close and the remaining development work are complete, and the Monitor said the build should take just under four years, which would put commissioning around 2031. Mr Younger said WPC looked forward to working with the arrangers to "conclude the financing process in the coming months".

WPC says the plant will supply mining companies, industry, commercial customers and households, create more than 100 permanent jobs and improve the reliability of supply across Western Province, where the 1972 line has long been a constraint. International Water Power noted that the scheme holds Africa's first Gold certification under the Hydropower Sustainability Standard. Ms Byrne said hydropower offered renewable baseload power and that partnerships between developers, commercial lenders, development finance institutions and local communities were essential to meeting the country's long-term energy needs.

body.title: Ngonye Falls at a glance
items: **Capacity** — 180MW, run-of-river, on the Zambezi in Western Province.
**Cost** — US$600 million (Zambia Monitor) or US$800 million (International Water Power).
**Grid link** — a 110km, 220kV line, replacing dependence on a 66kV line built in 1972.
**Arrangers** — Stanbic Bank Zambia and the DBSA, with Standard Bank South Africa also named by International Water Power.
**Timeline** — financial close in the coming months, construction from 2027, just under four years to build.

stories.title: Ten transformers in a week and four cathodes off a moving truck: ZESCO puts its latest vandalism losses at K1.2 million as police investigate a copper theft on the Livingstone road
stories.excerpt: ZESCO recorded 23 cases of vandalism between 31 October and 5 November, 15% more than the week before, and said the loss of ten pole-mounted transformers, only three of them recovered, pushed its net loss up 317% to K1,246,931, Zambia Monitor reported on Monday 9 November. Separately, Southern Province police are investigating the theft of four copper cathode plates from a truck travelling between the Kafue weighbridge and Mazabuka on Friday 6 November, News Diggers reported.

image.label: The vandalism ledger
image.caption: A week of transformer thefts cost the utility more than three times what the previous week did, even though the number of cases fell.

body: ZESCO's weekly vandalism report has become a measure of a different kind of load on the grid. In a statement issued in Lusaka on Monday 9 November and reported by Zambia Monitor, the utility said it had recorded 23 cases of vandalism of electricity infrastructure between 31 October and 5 November, 15% more than the 20 of the previous week. Ten pole-mounted transformers were damaged or stolen in the period and only three were recovered.

The money tells the story more sharply than the case count. ZESCO logged 25 security-related cases with estimated property losses of K1,760,001 and recoveries of K513,070, leaving a net loss of K1,246,931. The statement said that although the overall number of reported cases had fallen by about 7%, the net financial loss had risen by 317% compared with the previous week, mainly because of the value of the transformers taken. The Monitor noted that the report did not reconcile the 15% rise in vandalism cases with the 7% fall in overall cases, which appear to be counted on different bases.

body.text: Protecting electricity infrastructure is a shared responsibility.
body.attribution: ZESCO, in a statement issued in Lusaka on Monday 9 November, quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: The statement also reported two court outcomes. In Mansa on 3 November, a man pleaded guilty in the Resident Magistrate's Court to possessing property suspected of being stolen after police recovered 40 metres of aluminium conductor worth K5,520, which was returned to ZESCO; he was fined K6,000, or six months' imprisonment in default. In Mpulungu on 4 November, three children were found guilty of stealing ZESCO service cables worth K3,780; one was committed to Katombola reformatory school for 12 months and the other two were placed on six months' probation. ZESCO thanked the police and members of the public for the recoveries, and said theft and vandalism divert money that would otherwise go to improving the network and connecting new customers.

Copper leaves the country on the same roads the thieves use. News Diggers reported on Monday that four copper cathode plates were stolen from a moving truck on the Lusaka–Livingstone road between the Kafue weighbridge and Mazabuka district on Friday 6 November, between 17:40 and 19:30. The Southern Province Commanding Officer, Moono Namalongo, confirmed the incident in a statement and said police in Mazabuka were investigating a case of theft of goods in transit; the truck was carrying a consignment from Ndola. "The value of the stolen plates has not yet been ascertained," Ms Namalongo said. No arrest had been reported by Monday night.

stories.title: Three in a row: Barbra Banda is named in the FIFPRO Women's World 11 again, the only player in the team from outside England and Spain, chosen by 6,511 fellow professionals
stories.excerpt: FIFPRO announced the 2026 team on Monday 9 November, as scheduled. The Orlando Pride forward is one of three strikers alongside Barcelona's Claudia Pina and Arsenal's Alessia Russo, and her third selection extends her record as the African woman with the most World 11 appearances. Players from 64 countries voted on performances between 4 August 2025 and 16 August 2026, a period in which Banda scored 17 NWSL goals and broke the Pride's single-season record.

image.label: World 11, third time
image.caption: The Zambia forward is the only African player to be chosen for the players' team of the year more than once.

body: Barbra Banda has been voted into the FIFPRO Women's World 11 for the third year running. The global players' union announced the team on Monday 9 November, and the Zambia forward, who plays for Orlando Pride in the United States, is one of three forwards, with Claudia Pina of Barcelona and Alessia Russo of Arsenal. She is the only player in the eleven who does not play for England or Spain, FIFPRO said, and her third selection extends her record as the African woman with the most appearances in the team.

The rest of the side is drawn entirely from England and Spain: Hannah Hampton of Chelsea in goal; Lucy Bronze of Chelsea, Alex Greenwood of Manchester City, and Mapi León and Irene Paredes of Barcelona in defence; and Aitana Bonmatí, Alexia Putellas and Ella Toone in midfield. FIFPRO said 6,511 women's professionals from 64 countries took part in the vote, judging performances between 4 August 2025 and 16 August 2026. A player needed at least 20 official appearances to be eligible; each voter chose three players per position, and the eleven is made up of the top goalkeeper, three defenders, three midfielders, three forwards and the remaining outfield player with most votes.

Orlando Pride's own announcement set out why her fellow players chose her. In the 2026 NWSL season Banda scored 17 goals and added four assists in 23 appearances, the club's best return and, it said, tied for the fifth-highest goal involvement in a single season in the league's history. The 17 goals set a new Pride single-season record, passing the mark set by Marta in 2017, which Banda had equalled during the 2024 championship season; the record-breaking goal came against Houston Dash on 6 September. She is the only NWSL player in this year's World 11.

Banda first made the team in 2024, when she became the first African player to be selected, and remains the only African to have been chosen more than once, the club said. FIFPRO's figures for this year's vote are those for the women's award; Orlando Pride's release gave a combined figure of more than 26,000 voters across 75 countries, which appears to cover the men's and women's votes together.

stories.title: Eighteen in camp, eight more on the night flight and the bonuses finally moving: Chipolopolo settle into Ndola four days before Burundi
stories.excerpt: Albert Kangwanda flew in from Dar es Salaam on Monday 9 November to join a Zambia camp already holding 18 locally based players and the captain, Fashion Sakala, ZamFoot reported, with eight more foreign-based players due that night and George Lwandamina expected to trim the group to 26. The same day the sports ministry's permanent secretary, Kangwa Chileshe, told ZNBC that the government had begun paying the outstanding winning bonuses owed to Chipolopolo and the Copper Queens.

image.label: Levy Mwanawasa, 13 November
image.caption: Zambia are second in Group I, a point behind Algeria, before the double-header against bottom-placed Burundi.

body: Chipolopolo's camp for the Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Burundi is filling up in Ndola. Albert Kangwanda, the Young Africans striker, arrived from Dar es Salaam on Monday 9 November, ZamFoot reported, on the same flight as Derrick Mukombozi, the Burundi defender who plays for Fountain Gate in Tanzania and formerly turned out for Nkana and FC Leopards. Eighteen locally based players were already in camp and the captain, Fashion Sakala, had joined them; eight other foreign-based players were expected on Monday night.

The coach, George Lwandamina, is expected to cut his provisional squad to 26 once everyone is in, ZamFoot said. Some players who might have been considered are instead with the under-23 side, which plays Burkina Faso in Ouagadougou on Wednesday 11 November and again at Heroes Stadium in Lusaka four days later.

Zambia play Burundi at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Friday 13 November and in Bujumbura on Tuesday 17 November. Going into the double-header Zambia are second in Group I with three points from two games, one behind Algeria, with Togo also on three and Burundi bottom on one, ZamFoot reported. The group feeds AFCON 2027, which Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania will co-host from 19 June to 17 July next year.

There was news on money too. Kangwa Chileshe, the Permanent Secretary at the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts, told ZNBC Sports News on Monday that the government had started settling the outstanding winning bonuses owed to the men's and women's national teams and that payments were under way, ZamFoot reported. He said the exercise was meant to motivate players who represent the country abroad and to show the government's support ahead of the Burundi games, and asked Lwandamina's side to go for wins in both. The report gave no amounts, no number of players being paid and no date by which the arrears would be cleared, nor did it say how far back the unpaid bonuses go.

analysis.title: A treason charge is the start of a process, not the end of one
analysis.body: The police statement on Martha Mwitumwa is short and its gaps are the point. It names an offence, a period of almost a year and a place; it does not name the plan, the alleged accomplices or the evidence. That is normal at the charging stage, but it means the public has, so far, only the State's label. The 18 people charged in August are still waiting for a High Court ruling on bail after a hearing that was adjourned repeatedly, so the next stage for her may be slow. Two readings will compete. The government's, restated by Dr Andeleki on Friday, is that the law is being enforced against people who planned to take power unlawfully, and that opposition membership is not immunity. Critics', set out by Human Rights Watch this month, is that treason is being used broadly against people connected to the losing side. Monday's charge does not settle that argument; the particulars, when they are read in court, will tell more. Watch for the date of her first appearance, whether co-accused are named, and whether the August detention at a campaign media centre turns out to be part of the same file.

analysis.title: Both sides left the EU dialogue with what they came for
analysis.body: Zambia asked for Monday's meeting in September, when the European Parliament's resolution landed before the observers' final report. The request was a way of moving the argument from a chamber in Strasbourg, where Lusaka has no vote, to a table in Lusaka, where it is a party. On that measure it worked. Mr Haimbe secured a commitment to work through the mission's recommendations before 2031, a framing that treats the findings as technical improvements, and he asked for the government's comments to be heard before the final report is published. The EU, for its part, said in public and in Lusaka that grievances must go through fair and impartial courts, that it remains concerned about civic space, and that it will support a process of dialogue and reconciliation. Neither statement, as reported, mentioned the Mundubile trial, which the mission said last week it would follow and which the government spokesman says is none of its business. That silence is the thing to watch: whether the final report, and the EU's response to the treason cases, stay inside the frame agreed on Monday or step outside it.

analysis.title: Ngonye Falls has arrangers; the number to watch is the one the reports disagree on
analysis.body: A mandate letter is not money. What Western Power Company signed in Livingstone is an agreement that Stanbic and the DBSA will go and find the debt, and the developer's own description, the last step before financial close, is also an admission that close has not happened. The project has been in development long enough to have earned a sustainability certification and lost none of its logic: a 180MW plant in a province fed by a single 66kV line from 1972 would change what is possible there, from mining to household supply. Two things are unresolved. The first is the price: one report says US$600 million, another US$800 million, and the gap matters to how much debt must be raised and at what tariff ZESCO or private offtakers will pay. The second is timing: construction from 2027 and just under four years to build puts first power around 2031, after the next election and well after the current deficit. Watch for the financial close announcement the developer says is months away, the offtake arrangements, and whether the transmission line is financed with the plant or separately.
